result: Aphantasics were validated as having reduced visual imagery using both subjective (VVIQ) and objective (binocular rivalry task) measures. Aphantasics scored significantly lower on the VVIQ than controls and showed reduced priming effects in the binocular rivalry task, with controls showing above-chance performance while aphantasics did not.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly praised this as a major strength. One reviewer stated 'One of the major strengths of this study is the use of both self-report as well as objective measures to quantify imagery ability.' Another noted that 'Self-report as well as objective measures were used to establish that the aphantasia group indeed had lower imagery vividness than the control group.'

result: Aphantasics showed reduced autobiographical memory detail compared to controls, specifically reporting fewer internal details (including perceptual, emotional, temporal, and spatial details) but not external details. They also showed reduced episodic richness and memory confidence, and reported greater difficulty recalling memories and using imagination, but no difficulties with spatial orientation.
evaluation: Reviewers accepted these findings without challenge. One reviewer summarized: 'Results showed that participants with aphantasia reported significantly fewer internal details (but not external details) compared to controls; that they had lower confidence in their AMs.' The editor noted the study used 'a well-established interview paradigm' and reviewers praised the 'hypothesis-driven' analyses that 'reveal unambiguous results.'

result: Aphantasics showed reduced bilateral hippocampal activation during autobiographical memory retrieval compared to controls, with reductions observed across all four hippocampal subregions (left/right anterior/posterior), but no laterality or anterior-posterior gradient differences between groups.
evaluation: Reviewers accepted these findings as convincing evidence. One reviewer stated 'compared to controls, aphantasics had a reduction in activity in the hippocampus' and noted 'alterations in hippocampal and visual cortex processing seeming to underlie the deficits in autobiographical memory.' The editor described the evidence as 'convincing.'

result: During autobiographical memory retrieval, aphantasics displayed increased activation in bilateral visual-perceptual cortices (occipital lobe) compared to controls, while controls showed greater right hippocampal activation. A negative correlation was found between visual cortex and hippocampal activation, suggesting a trade-off between these regions.
evaluation: Reviewers accepted these findings without critique. One reviewer summarized: 'people with aphantasia displayed decreased hippocampal and increased visual-perceptual cortex activation during AM retrieval compared to controls' and noted these were 'unambiguous results.' The findings aligned with reviewers' understanding that 'the results are in line with the idea that aphantasia is caused by an increase in noise within the visual system.'

result: Controls showed strong negative functional connectivity between the right hippocampus and left visual-perceptual cortices during autobiographical memory retrieval, while aphantasics showed almost no functional connectivity between these regions.
evaluation: Reviewers accepted this finding as a key result. One reviewer stated 'For controls, these two regions were also functionally connected during autobiographical memory retrieval, which did not seem to be the case for aphantasics.' The editor noted the study 'sheds light on the neural underpinnings of episodic memory and mental imagery.'

result: Resting-state functional connectivity between the right hippocampus and visual cortex showed opposite relationships with visualization ability in the two groups: positive correlation in controls but negative correlation in aphantasics.
evaluation: Reviewers accepted this finding without challenge. One reviewer noted 'resting-state connectivity between visual cortex and hippocampus was positively related to autobiographical vividness in the control group but negatively in the aphantasia group.' This was treated as part of the convincing evidence package.

result: The authors conclude that visual mental imagery plays an important role in detail-rich vivid autobiographical memory, supported by functional connectivity between the hippocampus and visual-perceptual cortex. The deficit in aphantasia leads to broader impairments in episodic memory retrieval beyond just visual details.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly supported this conclusion. One reviewer stated 'The data provided good support for the conclusion that the authors draw, namely that there is a "tight link between visual imagery and our ability to retrieve vivid and detail-rich personal past events."' However, reviewers noted a limitation: 'the exact nature of this relationship is difficult to infer from this study alone, as the slow temporal resolution of fMRI cannot establish the directionality between the hippocampus and the visual-perceptual cortex.'

result: Aphantasics self-reported greater difficulty recalling memories and using imagination in daily life, but no difficulties with spatial orientation compared to controls.
evaluation: Reviewers raised concerns about the vagueness and potential limitations of these self-report questions. One reviewer noted 'A weakness of the study is that some of the questions used are a bit vague, and no objective measure is used' and specifically critiqued the spatial navigation question as not nuanced enough to distinguish between cognitive maps and landmarks. They also noted the imagination question 'could also be more nuanced' and that 'the general phrasing of "how difficult is [x]" could also potentially bias participants towards more negative answers.'

result: During the fMRI task, controls reported vivid memory retrieval in 86% of trials while aphantasics reported vividness in only 20% of trials. Aphantasics also responded slower when judging memory vividness, possibly reflecting uncertainty.
evaluation: Reviewers accepted these behavioral findings from the fMRI task without critique, treating them as supporting evidence for the main conclusions about memory differences between groups.

result: The authors propose mechanistic explanations for aphantasia-related memory deficits, including that heightened visual cortex activity hinders detection of imagery signals, that hippocampal signals may normally inhibit sensory noise in visual cortex, and that the top-down hierarchy between hippocampus and visual cortex is disrupted in aphantasia.
evaluation: Reviewers accepted these interpretations as reasonable theoretical frameworks consistent with the data. One reviewer noted the results 'are in line with the idea that aphantasia is caused by an increase in noise within the visual system combined with a decrease in top-down communication from the hippocampus.' However, reviewers acknowledged these remain speculative given fMRI's temporal limitations.

result: The authors draw parallels between aphantasics and individuals with hippocampal damage, noting both show reduced internal memory details across subcategories regardless of memory recency. However, aphantasics differ in that spatial abilities appear intact, suggesting some hippocampal processes remain functional.
evaluation: Reviewers accepted this comparison and noted its theoretical importance. One reviewer stated 'Future work could also build on the interesting findings regarding spatial navigation, which together with previous findings in aphantasia...strongly suggests that spatial abilities in people with aphantasia are unaffected. This can shed further light on the different neural pathways of spatial and object memory in general.'
